opus-5.5.text:
I think the claim that pretraining scaling has "hit a wall" is a bit oversimplified. What's really happening is that the easy part of the curve is behind us. Early on, you could add compute and data and get very visible jumps in capability almost for free. Now the marginal gains from pure pretraining are more expensive. High-quality text on the internet is finite, and the improvements on many benchmarks look smaller in absolute terms. So people feel it's slowing down.

But "harder" is different from "over." Scaling laws were never a promise of infinite free lunch. They describe a smooth relationship between resources and loss, and as far as I can tell that relationship hasn't broken. What has changed is the economics: the cost per unit of improvement is going up, and the bottleneck has shifted from compute toward data, both its quantity and its quality.

I also think the more interesting change is that pretraining is no longer the only lever. In the past few years we've seen that you can get huge gains from post-training, reinforcement learning, and especially from scaling compute at inference time: letting the model think longer, search, use tools, verify its own work. Pretraining gives you a strong prior, a broad base of knowledge and intuition. RL and test-time compute teach the model how to actually use that knowledge to solve hard problems. These are complementary, not competing.

So my view is: pretraining scaling still matters, and a stronger base model makes everything downstream work better. But the frontier of progress has moved. If you only look at pretraining loss curves, you might conclude things are plateauing. If you look at what models can actually do on reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks, progress is arguably faster than ever. The question isn't whether scaling is dead. It's which axis you're scaling, and how you combine them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the framing itself is a little off. People say "pretraining has hit a wall," but what actually happened is more specific: the easy part of scaling ended. For a few years, the recipe was simple — more data, more compute, bigger model, and the loss goes down predictably. That curve is still real. The problem is that the inputs became the bottleneck, not the law. We've roughly run through the high-quality text on the internet, and compute is growing, but you can't double it every six months forever. So the law didn't break; we just ran out of cheap things to feed it.

The second thing is that loss going down and capability going up are not the same thing. Lower perplexity on web text gives you a better and better prior over human language, but at some point the marginal gain in what the model can actually do — solve a hard math problem, debug a codebase, plan a multi-step task — gets smaller relative to what you'd get from spending that same compute elsewhere. That "elsewhere" is reinforcement learning, test-time compute, letting the model reason longer and act in an environment. That's where I think the frontier has moved.

I'd describe it this way: pretraining builds the prior, and RL and interaction build the agent. The prior matters enormously — you can't do RL on a weak base model and expect much — so I don't think pretraining is dead or irrelevant. It's just no longer the only lever. The question for the next few years isn't "how big can we make the model," it's "what environments, what tasks, what reward signals do we train against, and how do we scale those." That's a much harder engineering and research problem, honestly, because there's no single number you can just crank up. Each domain needs its own environment.

So my short answer is: the scaling law for pretraining is fine, the easy scaling is over, and the interesting work has moved to a different axis.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish two claims. One is that pretraining has reached a fundamental limit. The other is that scaling pretraining alone is no longer the most effective way to improve AI. Those are quite different, and I’m more sympathetic to the second.

A scaling law describes how something like prediction loss changes as you increase compute, data, and model size. It doesn’t guarantee that every reduction in loss translates into an equally valuable improvement in real-world tasks. So you can have continued progress on the pretraining objective while the practical returns become less obvious.

There are also constraints around data and cost. But hitting a constraint in the current recipe doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve discovered a fundamental ceiling on learning.

What interests me more is how we expand the recipe. Pretraining gives a model a foundation, but a system can also improve through interaction, feedback, and spending more computation on a problem at inference time. For an agent, the question isn’t just whether it can predict the next token. It’s whether it can take an action, observe the result, and make progress toward a goal.

So I wouldn’t say pretraining is finished. I’d say we should stop treating pretraining scale as the only axis of progress. The important question is where the next unit of compute produces the most useful improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish two claims: that pretraining has diminishing returns, and that scaling has reached a hard limit. Those are quite different. If getting the next improvement requires much more compute or data, that makes progress more expensive; it doesn’t necessarily mean progress has stopped.

I also wouldn’t equate the limits of pretraining with the limits of AI. Pretraining gives you a strong starting point, but there are other ways to improve a system: post-training, letting it spend more computation reasoning, or letting it interact with an environment and learn from feedback.

For me, an interesting question is how we move from learning from static text to learning through actions. If a model writes code, runs it, observes an error, and fixes it, there’s a feedback loop there. The challenge becomes how to turn those interactions into reliable learning.

So I’m skeptical of the strongest version of the claim. Pretraining might become a less dominant source of progress without scaling as a whole coming to an end. We should ask what we’re scaling, and whether that additional computation translates into better performance on tasks people actually care about.
